name: WASI
vendor: WASI Subgroup of the W3C WebAssembly Community Group
license: Open standard, published under the W3C Community Contributor License Agreement
summary: The WebAssembly System Interface: standard APIs for files, clocks, random numbers, sockets and HTTP that let one `.wasm` binary run outside the browser, with only the capabilities its host grants.
intro: A WebAssembly module can’t do anything outside its own memory except call the functions its host passes in. WASI standardises those functions for hosts other than a browser, so a program compiled once runs on any runtime that implements them, on any operating system and CPU. Programs run in a capability-based sandbox: they start with no ambient authority, so there is no global file system or network to reach. The host hands in what it chooses, such as one directory (`wasmtime --dir .`) or an outgoing HTTP client.

There have been three milestone releases. Preview 1 (WASI 0.1, 2019) is a POSIX-like set of functions, modelled on CloudABI, that a core module imports from a module named `wasi_snapshot_preview1`; it is still widely used, but frozen. WASI 0.2 (January 2024) started again on top of the Component Model: interfaces are written in WIT, with strings, records and resources instead of raw pointers, and grouped into worlds such as `wasi:cli/command` for command-line programs and `wasi:http/proxy` for HTTP handlers. WASI 0.3.0 (11 June 2026) replaced 0.2’s hand-built streams and polling (`wasi:io`) with the Component Model’s native async: functions are `async func`, and data flows as `stream<T>` and `future<T>`. The HTTP world became `service`, a new `middleware` world was added, and the sockets interfaces shrank from seven to two.

Releases follow a train: a patch release every two months, 0.2.1 through 0.2.12 and then 0.3.1 (August 2026) and 0.3.2 (13 October 2026). Wasmtime 46 was the first runtime to implement the final 0.3.0, and jco runs 0.3 components in JavaScript hosts. Rust has a target for each generation: `wasm32-wasip1` emits core modules, `wasm32-wasip2` emits components, and `wasm32-wasip3` is an experimental tier 3 target.
strengths: One binary for every operating system and CPU the runtime supports, with no recompiling
Capability-based: a program gets only the directories, sockets and HTTP clients the host grants, which suits plugins and untrusted code
WIT interfaces with rich types, so components written in Rust, Go, C or JavaScript can call each other without hand-written glue
Since 0.3, async is part of the Component Model itself, so concurrent I/O doesn’t depend on each language’s own runtime
limits: Still pre-1.0: interfaces are versioned (`@0.3.2`), and a mismatch between the WIT version a component was built against and the one the runtime provides fails at instantiation with a type error
Three generations in use at once: many tools and hosts still support only preview 1, which gets no new APIs or documentation
Covers a subset of an operating system: no `fork`, and interfaces such as key-value stores, messaging, SQL and GPU are still proposals in phase 1 or 2
Support varies by host: Cloudflare Workers implements only some WASI calls, and browsers run components only after jco translates them to JavaScript

story: Once WebAssembly worked in browsers, people wanted to run it on servers and devices, but there was no standard way for a module to open a file or read the clock. Early runtimes imitated the JavaScript glue that the Emscripten compiler generated, which Lin Clark of Mozilla described as “emulating an internal detail of an emulation layer of POSIX”. On 27 March 2019 Mozilla announced WASI and chartered a subgroup of the WebAssembly Community Group to standardise it, with Fastly as a partner. Three implementations existed at launch: Mozilla’s Wasmtime, Fastly’s Lucet and a browser polyfill.

Preview 1 was closely derived from CloudABI and based on POSIX, which made it biased towards C: raw pointers and implied data structures. Rather than keep extending it, the subgroup rebuilt WASI on the Component Model, and on 25 January 2024 voted to launch WASI 0.2, which Dan Gohman called “a milestone along the way, rather than a destination”. Its successor, 0.3.0, shipped on 11 June 2026 as an exception to the release train approved by a subgroup vote, after release candidates in early 2026, and moved async into the Component Model. No date has been set for WASI 1.0.

choices.why: Following CloudABI and Capsicum, a module gets handles with permissions attached instead of opening any path it likes, so a host can grant one directory and nothing else, and narrow access further as handles are passed on.
A small device and a cloud server can’t offer the same APIs, so WASI is split into separate proposals (files, clocks, sockets, HTTP) that a platform implements only where they make sense.

Preview 1’s C-style pointers and implied layouts made it awkward for other languages and impossible to virtualise. WIT interfaces with rich types let any language bind to WASI, and let one component provide an interface to another.

In 0.2 every interface threaded I/O through `wasi:io` pollables and explicit streams. Making `future` and `stream` part of the Component Model lets interfaces declare `async func` directly and lets the host run many calls concurrently.

timeline.text: Mozilla announces WASI in March; preview 1 becomes the first API
WASI 0.2, built on the Component Model, launched on 25 January; Rust renames `wasm32-wasi` to `wasm32-wasip1` in March
WASI 0.3.0 adds native async on 11 June; 0.3.2 on 13 October
